source.title: HunyuanVideo: A Systematic Framework For Large Video Generative Models
source.authors: Wei-Jie Kong; Qi Tian; Zi-Jian Zhang; Rox Min; Zuozhuo Dai; Jin Zhou; Jia-Liang Xiong; Xin Li; Bo Wu; Jian-Wei Zhang; Kathrina Wu; Qin Lin; Junkun Yuan; Yan-Xin Long; Aladdin Wang; Andong Wang; Changlin Li; Duojun Huang; Fang Yang; Hao Tan; Hongmei Wang; Jacob Song; Jiawang Bai; Jian-Bing Wu; Jinbao Xue; Joey Wang; Kai Wang; Meng-Yang Liu; Peng-Yuan Li; Shuai Li; Wei-Yan Wang; Wenqing Yu; Xin-Chi Deng; Yang Li; Yi Chen; Yutao Cui; Yuanbo Peng; Zhen Yu; Zhiyu He; Zhi-Yong Xu; Zi-Xiang Zhou; Zunnan Xu; Yang-Dan Tao; Qing-Lin Lu; Song-Tao Liu; Da-Quan Zhou; Hong-Fa Wang; Yong Yang; Di Wang; Yuhong Liu; Jie Jiang; Caesar Zhong

record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling behavior for image and video diffusion models, extending scaling-law claims to other modalities and training regimes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports image and video scaling experiments and compute-optimal parameter/token allocation fits. It does not test held-out language-model cross-entropy, small-run prediction of much larger runs, architecture-shape effects, downstream-task predictability, or whether language-model scaling exponents depend on fitting choices. The text also cites language-model scaling results, which are not recorded as findings from this study.
record.test_reason: The study fits Hoffmann-style compute-optimal power laws (N_opt and D_opt against C) for text-to-image and text-to-video diffusion transformers. This is a new modality and setting with its own results bearing on V5. It does not study language models, so V1–V4, V6 and V7 as stated for LMs are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors fit Hoffmann-style compute-optimal power laws for N and D: first for text-to-image DiT models, then for video models initialised from image checkpoints. They combine these with training and inference cost to choose a 13B model and set first-stage token counts. Scaling of progressive resolution training is left to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The paper says it follows Hoffmann et al.'s experiment method, but studies diffusion-transformer image and video generation rather than language-model cross-entropy; it fits compute-optimal model and dataset sizes from loss envelopes.
record.method_sensitivity: The image and video fits have different reported coefficients. The video models are initialized from corresponding optimal image checkpoints.

fits_no_version.finding: Compute-optimal split differs sharply by modality. Image: N exponent 0.56 vs D exponent 0.43 (model grows faster). Video: N 0.36 vs D 0.63 (data grows faster).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In visual diffusion models, the compute-optimal parameter/data split depends on modality and initialisation, so no single allocation rule transfers across settings.

record.problems: The reported experiments concern diffusion-model scaling rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy. The text gives fitted coefficients but no uncertainty estimates. It states that progressive low-to-high-resolution training scaling is left unexplored.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported scaling results bearing on the tested versions were left out.

untested.parts: Repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes. Also a direct power-law fit of loss against compute, parameters or data in image/video: only the allocation exponents are reported. Scaling of the progressive low-to-high-resolution training is explicitly left to future work.
All of it for language models. The diffusion allocation fits do not bear on whether LM-optimal N and D grow equally or N faster.
Held-out LM pretraining loss power law.
Prediction of much larger runs. The 13B choice is made from the fits, but its realised loss is never compared with a prediction.
Shape effects at fixed parameter count.
Downstream predictability from scale or loss.
LM fit-dependence. No fitting-method or schedule comparisons are made.

missing.what: Claim that the chosen scaling strategy reduces compute 'by up to 5×' for the same performance; no supporting numbers or experiment are given.
Training-loss curves and envelopes against compute for each model size; the loss itself is not fitted as a power law in C.

record.verdict_notes: This is a technical report on a video foundation model; scaling laws occupy one subsection, with no confidence intervals, no held-out loss, and no check of the extrapolated 13B run. The study is not an original source. The record's V3 links were dropped because V3's subject is language models.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy for language models.
Whether fits from small runs predict the losses of runs orders of magnitude larger.
Language-model compute-optimal allocation and whether parameter and token counts grow equally in that setting.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Modalities and regimes beyond the image and video diffusion-model scaling experiments reported here, including repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
Predictability of downstream-task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Whether fitting choices cause published laws to disagree or curves to bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: DiT-T2X(I) family
rows.stage_stated: Image scaling experiment; models trained at 256px resolution
rows.operation_detail: Fit compute-optimal model parameter count as a power law in compute using the envelope of lowest-loss points.

conditions.value: DDPM and v-prediction, consistent hyperparameters and same dataset

rows.value: N_opt = a1 C^b1; a1 = 5.48 × 10^-4, b1 = 0.5634. Units of a1 and N_opt are billions; C is in Peta FLOPs.
rows.note: The authors state that the image-model family fits the power law quite well and use the fitted relation to calculate optimal model size for a compute budget.
rows.check: V3 removed: V3 concerns language-model compute-optimal allocation, and this is a diffusion image model. The fit uses training-loss envelopes (Fig. 10a y-axis 'Training Loss'), not held-out loss. The authors say only that it 'fits the power law quite well', with no goodness-of-fit or uncertainty.
